los.text: Describe and understand the classification of epilepsy according to seizure type and aetiology
los.html:
• Epilepsy (ILAE): two or more unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one unprovoked seizure with a high (≥60%) recurrence risk, or an epilepsy syndrome.
Seizure type (ILAE 2017)Subtypes
Focal onset (one hemisphere)Aware or impaired awareness; motor or non-motor onset; focal to bilateral tonic–clonic
Generalised onset (both hemispheres from the start)Motor: tonic–clonic, myoclonic, atonic, tonic, clonic; non-motor: absence
Unknown onset
  • Epilepsy types: focal, generalised, combined generalised and focal, unknown.
SyndromeFeatures
Childhood absence epilepsyBrief staring spells, many a day, 3 Hz spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsyTeenagers; morning myoclonic jerks, GTCS, absences; triggered by sleep deprivation, alcohol; lifelong
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)Clusters of flexion spasms, hypsarrhythmia, developmental regression; tuberous sclerosis
Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikesChildren; nocturnal focal facial seizures; outgrown
Temporal lobe epilepsyOften hippocampal sclerosis; aura, automatisms
Lennox–Gastaut, DravetSevere, drug-resistant, developmental impairment
  • Aetiology: structural (stroke, tumour, trauma, malformations, hippocampal sclerosis), genetic, infectious (encephalitis, neurocysticercosis), metabolic, immune (autoimmune encephalitis), unknown.
    • Provoked seizures: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, alcohol withdrawal, drugs, sleep deprivation.

los.text: Identify the key features in the history of a person presenting with transient loss of consciousness
los.html:
• An eyewitness account is vital (ask them to film any further episodes).
PhaseAsk
Before
  • Situation (standing, sitting, lying, exercise, prolonged standing, toilet, pain, emotion), sleep deprivation, alcohol, drugs, flashing lights
  • Prodrome (light-headed, sweaty, nauseous, vision greying: syncope)
  • Aura (déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, smell: focal seizure)
  • Palpitations or chest pain (cardiac)
DuringDuration, colour (pale vs cyanosed), eyes open or closed, movements (rhythmic, jerks, asynchronous), lateral tongue biting, incontinence, responsiveness, head turning, automatisms
AfterRecovery: rapid (syncope) vs prolonged confusion/drowsiness (postictal), headache, aching muscles, Todd's paresis, injuries
Background
  • Previous episodes, febrile seizures, head injury, meningitis
  • Cardiac history
  • Family history of sudden death under 40
  • Drugs (QT-prolonging, antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics)
  • Driving and occupation
Red flags for cardiac syncope(urgent cardiology)
  • Exertional syncope
  • Syncope while lying
  • Palpitations or chest pain beforehand
  • Family history of sudden cardiac death
  • Abnormal ECG (long QT, Brugada, WPW, heart block)
  • Structural heart disease
  • New breathlessness.
Every TLoC patient needsFull examination, lying and standing BP, 12-lead ECG, glucose; then refer appropriately (first seizure → specialist within 2 weeks).

los.text: Recognise and distinguish seizure from syncope and dissociative attacks and recognise different seizure types
los.html:
FeatureGeneralised tonic–clonic seizureSyncopeDissociative (functional) seizure
TriggerSleep deprivation, alcohol, flashing lightsPosture, prolonged standing, pain, micturition, emotion; exercise (cardiac)Stress (often none apparent)
WarningAura (focal onset) or noneLight-headed, sweaty, nauseous, tunnel visionVariable
EyesOpenOpenOften closed (resists opening)
ColourCyanosedPaleNormal
MovementsRhythmic, synchronous tonic then clonic, 1–3 minBrief irregular jerks (<15 s, "convulsive syncope")Asynchronous, side-to-side head shaking, pelvic thrusting, waxing and waning, often prolonged
TongueLateral bitingRareTip, or none
RecoveryPostictal confusion, drowsiness, headache, myalgiaQuickVariable; may cry, may recall the event
  • Gold standard: video EEG telemetry capturing a typical event.
Seizure typeFeatures
AbsenceBrief (5–10 s) staring, unresponsive, then immediate recovery, many a day; children
MyoclonicSudden brief jerks, often morning (JME)
AtonicSudden loss of tone ("drop attacks")
Focal awareMotor (Jacksonian march), sensory, autonomic, déjà vu, smells
Focal impaired awarenessTemporal lobe: aura, staring, lip-smacking/fiddling automatisms, postictal confusion
Focal to bilateral tonic–clonicFocal start then generalises

los.text: Describe the mode of action, indication and side effects of the common drugs used to treat epilepsy and status epilepticus in children and adults
sessions: Diagnosis, treatment epilepsy and status epilepticus
los.html:
DrugMechanismUseKey side effects
Sodium valproateNa⁺ channels, ↑ GABA, T-type Ca²⁺Broad spectrum: generalised epilepsies (JME, absence, GTCS) in males and those who can't become pregnant
  • Highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, developmental disorders): Pregnancy Prevention Programme
  • MHRA also restricts starting in younger men
  • Weight gain, hair loss, tremor, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, hyperammonaemia
LamotrigineNa⁺ channel blockerFocal and generalised; first choice for many women of childbearing potentialRash (SJS): slow titration (slower with valproate); levels fall in pregnancy and with oestrogen pills; may worsen myoclonus
LevetiracetamBinds SV2AFocal and generalised; IV in status; preferred in pregnancyMood changes, irritability, depression, psychosis
CarbamazepineNa⁺ channel blocker; enzyme inducerFocal; trigeminal neuralgiaHyponatraemia, rash/SJS (HLA-B*1502), leucopenia, ataxia, diplopia, reduces the pill's efficacy; worsens absence/myoclonic seizures
PhenytoinNa⁺ channel blockerStatus epilepticus (IV); rarely long-termZero-order kinetics, narrow therapeutic index; gum hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, nystagmus, neuropathy, osteomalacia; IV: arrhythmias, hypotension (cardiac monitoring)
EthosuximideT-type Ca²⁺ channels (thalamus)Absence seizures onlyGI upset
TopiramateMultipleFocal/generalised; migraineWeight loss, kidney stones, word-finding problems, teratogenic, glaucoma
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam)GABA-AStatus, clustersRespiratory depression
NICE NG217 first choices
  • Generalised tonic–clonic: valproate (if not of childbearing potential), otherwise lamotrigine or levetiracetam
  • Focal: lamotrigine or levetiracetam
  • Absence: ethosuximide
  • Myoclonic: valproate or levetiracetam.
  • Avoid carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin in absence/myoclonic epilepsy.
Status epilepticus(seizure ≥5 min, or repeated without recovery)
TimeAction
0–5 minABC, oxygen, check glucose, IV access, bloods, time it; thiamine if alcohol misuse
5 min
  • Benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg), or buccal midazolam 10 mg / rectal diazepam if no IV
  • Repeat once after 5–10 min
~20 min (established)Second line IV: levetiracetam (60 mg/kg, max 4.5 g), phenytoin (20 mg/kg, with cardiac monitoring) or valproate (40 mg/kg)
~40 min (refractory)Anaesthetist/ICU: rapid sequence induction (propofol or thiopental), EEG monitoring
  • Advice: driving (DVLA car licence: usually 6 months off after a first unprovoked seizure with normal investigations, 12 months seizure-free for epilepsy; stricter for HGV), safety (showers not baths, supervised swimming, heights, cooking), SUDEP (adherence, nocturnal seizures), contraception (enzyme inducers reduce hormonal methods: use IUD/IUS or injection), pregnancy (folic acid 5 mg, pre-conception review, lamotrigine level monitoring), bone health, withdrawing drugs only after ≥2 years seizure-free, slowly.

los.text: Describe the mode of inheritance and clinical features of common neurogenetic conditions and link to the current knowledge of the relevant genetic mutations and their pathological consequence.
los.html:
ConditionInheritanceGene / mutationClinical features
Huntington's diseaseAutosomal dominant, anticipation (especially paternal)CAG repeat in HTT (chromosome 4): ≥40 fully penetrant; toxic polyglutamine protein → caudate/striatal neuron lossChorea, psychiatric symptoms, dementia; onset 30–50; predictive testing with counselling
Myotonic dystrophy type 1AD, anticipation (maternal: congenital form)CTG repeat in DMPK (toxic RNA)Myotonia (can't let go of a handshake), distal weakness, ptosis, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, diabetes, hypogonadism
Duchenne muscular dystrophyX-linked recessiveDMD: out-of-frame deletions → no dystrophin (Becker: in-frame, milder)Boys aged 2–5: proximal weakness, Gowers' sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, very high CK; wheelchair by ~12, cardiomyopathy, respiratory failure
Spinal muscular atrophyAutosomal recessiveSMN1 deletion (SMN2 copy number modifies severity)Anterior horn cell loss: floppy infant, weakness, tongue fasciculations; nusinersen, risdiplam, gene therapy
Friedreich's ataxiaARGAA repeat in FXN (frataxin)Teen onset ataxia, absent reflexes with upgoing plantars, pes cavus, scoliosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes
Neurofibromatosis type 1AD (~50% new mutations)NF1 (neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor regulating Ras)≥6 café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, scoliosis, learning difficulties
NF2ADNF2 (merlin)Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas
Tuberous sclerosisADTSC1/TSC2 (mTOR pathway)Infantile spasms, epilepsy, learning disability, autism, ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma
Charcot–Marie–Tooth (1A)ADPMP22 duplication (demyelinating)Distal wasting ("inverted champagne bottle" legs), pes cavus, foot drop
Fragile XX-linkedCGG repeat in FMR1 (>200 → silencing)Learning disability, autism, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism
Dravet syndromeUsually de novoSCN1A loss of function (inhibitory interneurons)Prolonged febrile seizures in infancy, regression; avoid Na⁺ channel blockers
  • Key concepts: anticipation (repeat expansions lengthen → earlier, more severe disease in later generations)
    • penetrance
    • variable expressivity
    • de novo mutations
    • carrier and predictive testing
    • non-directive genetic counselling
    • new genetic therapies (antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapy).

los.text: Describe how the clinical presentation of neurological disease links with pathology
los.html:
• Neurological diagnosis asks where (localisation) and what (pathology, from the time course).
WhereClinical pattern
CortexDysphasia, neglect, seizures, cortical sensory loss, visual field defects
Subcortical white matter / internal capsulePure motor or sensory deficits, dense hemiparesis
BrainstemCrossed signs (cranial nerve on one side, limbs on the other), diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria
CerebellumIpsilateral ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor
Spinal cordSensory level, bilateral UMN signs, sphincter problems
Root / plexus / nerveDermatomal/myotomal; nerve distribution; LMN signs
Neuromuscular junctionFatigable weakness, no sensory loss
MuscleProximal symmetrical weakness, no sensory loss
What (time course)Pathology
Sudden (seconds–minutes)Vascular (stroke, haemorrhage), seizure
Acute (hours–days)Infection, inflammation, demyelination
Subacute (weeks)Tumour, inflammatory
Chronic progressive (months–years)Neurodegeneration, slow tumours
Relapsing–remittingMS
ParoxysmalEpilepsy, migraine
  • Pathology → signs: infarction in a vascular territory → sudden focal deficit
    • mass lesion → progressive deficit, seizures, raised ICP (headache, papilloedema)
    • demyelination → conduction block, multifocal relapses, worse with heat
    • neurodegeneration (protein aggregates: amyloid and tau in Alzheimer's, α-synuclein in Parkinson's, TDP-43 in MND) → gradual selective decline
    • loss of descending inhibition → spasticity and brisk reflexes (UMN)
    • denervation → wasting and fasciculation (LMN)
    • cortical irritation → seizures.

los.text: Identify the key clinical features of a person presenting in coma and link to a relevant differential diagnosis, investigation and management plan.
los.html:
• Coma: unrousable unresponsiveness (GCS ≤8: protect the airway).
AssessmentFindings and meaning
GCS (E4, V5, M6)Severity, trend
PupilsPinpoint: opioids, pontine haemorrhage; unilateral fixed dilated: III compression (uncal herniation); bilateral fixed dilated: severe hypoxic injury, anticholinergics, brainstem death
Eye movementsOculocephalic (doll's eye) reflex tests brainstem integrity; conjugate deviation towards a hemispheric lesion
BreathingCheyne–Stokes (bilateral hemisphere/diencephalon), Kussmaul (metabolic acidosis: DKA), ataxic (medulla)
PostureDecorticate (flexion: above the midbrain), decerebrate (extension: midbrain/pons, worse)
Lateralising signsHemiparesis, asymmetric reflexes or plantars → structural lesion
Other clues
  • Meningism
  • Papilloedema
  • Rash (meningococcus)
  • Needle marks
  • Cherry-red skin (CO)
  • Breath (ketones, alcohol, fetor hepaticus, uraemia)
  • Temperature
  • Cushing's response
  • Head injury signs (Battle's sign, raccoon eyes)
  • MedicAlert
CauseExamples
StructuralHaemorrhage, basilar thrombosis, tumour, subdural/extradural haematoma, abscess
MetabolicHypoglycaemia, DKA/HHS, hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, uraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypothermia, myxoedema
ToxicOpioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, tricyclics, carbon monoxide
InfectionMeningitis, encephalitis, sepsis
SeizuresNon-convulsive status, postictal state
Investigations
  • Capillary glucose immediately
  • ABG/VBG
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • LFT
  • Calcium
  • Ammonia
  • CK
  • Cultures
  • Paracetamol and salicylate levels
  • Alcohol
  • Toxicology
  • ECG
  • Urgent CT head
  • LP (if CT safe and infection or SAH suspected)
  • EEG (non-convulsive status)
  • MRI.
Management
  • ABCDE
  • Airway protection (anaesthetist, intubation if GCS ≤8), recovery position, oxygen
  • Treat hypoglycaemia (IV glucose; thiamine with it if alcohol misuse/malnutrition)
  • Naloxone if opioid toxicity suspected
  • Empirical ceftriaxone + aciclovir if infection possible
  • Treat seizures
  • Correct metabolic causes
  • Neurosurgery for haematoma or hydrocephalus
  • Raised ICP measures (head up 30°, osmotherapy)
  • ICU and supportive care (pressure areas, eyes, catheter, VTE prophylaxis).

los.text: Engage in a gamified interactive review session that reinforces and consolidates knowledge covered in the curriculum
los.html:
• Gamified review: test yourself on high-yield Year 2 topics in this app's quiz (daily, due reviews, shaky) and note gaps.
Quick-fire checklist
Interpreting U&Es, FBC, LFTs, TFTs, ABGs, ECGs
A–E for sepsis, asthma, DKA, status epilepticus, anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest
Prescribing: opioids and CDs, insulin, anticoagulants, antibiotics, fluids, renal dosing
Core examinations and presenting findings
Communication: breaking bad news, MI, capacity, consent, safeguarding

los.text: Elicit a comprehensive history from an older adult presenting with depression,
sessions: History depression with an older patient
los.html:
• Older adults often present atypically: physical complaints (pain, tiredness, poor appetite)
    • anxiety
    • irritability
    • memory complaints ("depressive pseudodementia")
    • weight loss
    • self-neglect or withdrawal
    • rather than describing sadness.
AreaQuestions
Core symptomsLow mood, anhedonia, low energy for ≥2 weeks
BiologicalSleep (early waking), appetite, weight loss, psychomotor slowing, libido, diurnal variation
CognitiveConcentration, memory, guilt, worthlessness, hopelessness
Psychotic featuresNihilistic or poverty delusions, hallucinations
Risk
  • Suicidal thoughts, plans, means (stockpiled medicines), previous attempts
  • Older men have the highest suicide rates
  • Isolation, bereavement, chronic illness and pain, alcohol
  • Also self-neglect, safeguarding
TriggersBereavement, loss of independence, retirement, new diagnosis, moving into care
Physical and drugsChronic illness, pain, sensory loss; drugs (beta-blockers, steroids, benzodiazepines, levodopa, opioids)
Function and socialADLs, living alone, carers, finances, loneliness
BackgroundPast psychiatric history, family history, alcohol
  • Tools: Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), PHQ-9; cognitive screen to separate depression from dementia; collateral history with consent.

los.text: Identify and exclude potential physical causes of mood changes (e.g. thyroid dysfunction, vitamin deficiencies)
sessions: History depression with an older patient
los.html:
Physical causeTest
Hypothyroidism (and apathetic hyperthyroidism)TFTs
B12/folate deficiency, anaemiaB12, folate, FBC
Hypercalcaemia ("moans and groans")Calcium
Hyponatraemia, CKD, liver diseaseU&E, LFT
DiabetesGlucose/HbA1c
Infection (UTI, HIV, syphilis)Urine dip if symptomatic, serology if at risk
Cushing's, Addison'sCortisol tests if clinical clues
Neurological: dementia, post-stroke, Parkinson's, MS, frontal tumourCognitive testing, CT/MRI if neurological signs
Malignancy (e.g. pancreatic), chronic pain, sleep apnoeaAs indicated
Medications (beta-blockers, steroids, isotretinoin, levetiracetam, benzodiazepines, opioids) and alcoholMedication review, AUDIT
  • Why: treating the physical cause may relieve the mood problem, and depressive symptoms can be the first sign of serious illness.

los.text: Interpret liver function test (LFT) results, integrating the findings with clinical information to guide patient management
los.html:
TestSource / meaning
ALTHepatocytes (liver-specific): hepatocellular injury
ASTLiver, muscle, heart, red cells
ALPBiliary epithelium, bone, placenta, gut
GGTBiliary; induced by alcohol and enzyme-inducing drugs; confirms a raised ALP is from the liver
BilirubinUnconjugated (pre-hepatic) or conjugated (hepatic/obstructive)
AlbuminSynthetic function (half-life ~3 weeks: chronic disease); also low in malnutrition, sepsis, nephrotic syndrome
PT/INRSynthetic function (clotting factors, short half-life: acute liver failure); vitamin K deficiency
Approach
  • (1) pattern (hepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed, isolated bilirubin)
  • (2) magnitude
  • (3) synthetic function (albumin, INR, platelets: severity)
  • (4) clinical context (alcohol, drugs, symptoms, risk factors)
  • (5) next tests: ultrasound + non-invasive liver screen (hepatitis B and C serology, autoantibodies: ANA, ASMA, AMA; immunoglobulins; ferritin and transferrin saturation; caeruloplasmin in younger patients; α1-antitrypsin; coeliac serology; HbA1c, lipids)
  • (6) fibrosis assessment (FIB-4, ELF test, FibroScan).
R ratio(ALT ÷ ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ULN): ≥5 hepatocellular, ≤2 cholestatic, 2–5 mixed.

los.text: Recognise common patterns of abnormal LFT results (e.g. hepatocellular, cholestatic) and apply appropriate differential diagnoses
los.html:
PatternDifferential
Hepatocellular, very high ALT (>1000)Viral hepatitis (A, B, E), paracetamol overdose, ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), autoimmune hepatitis, acute stone passage (transient), Wilson's
Hepatocellular, modest
  • MASLD (ALT > AST), alcohol (AST:ALT >2, high GGT, macrocytosis), chronic hepatitis B/C, drugs (statins), haemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, coeliac disease
  • Muscle injury (AST with high CK)
Cholestatic (ALP + GGT ≫ ALT)
  • Extrahepatic: gallstones in the CBD, pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, strictures, PSC (IBD, beaded ducts on MRCP).
  • Intrahepatic: PBC (middle-aged women, itch, AMA positive, raised IgM: ursodeoxycholic acid)
  • Drugs (co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, chlorpromazine, oestrogens)
  • Infiltration (metastases, lymphoma, sarcoid)
  • Cholestasis of pregnancy
  • Sepsis
Isolated raised ALP, normal GGTBone (Paget's, metastases, osteomalacia, healing fracture, adolescent growth), pregnancy (placental)
Isolated raised GGTAlcohol, enzyme-inducing drugs, MASLD
Isolated unconjugated bilirubinGilbert's syndrome (benign), haemolysis (check FBC, reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin)
Low albumin, high INR, low plateletsCirrhosis (synthetic failure + hypersplenism); a high INR alone may be vitamin K deficiency (corrects with IV vitamin K)
  • Next step: hepatocellular → ultrasound and liver screen
    • cholestatic → ultrasound: dilated ducts → MRCP, CT, ERCP
    • non-dilated → AMA, drug review, consider biopsy.

los.text: Identify the basal ganglia and their main functions, and connections to other parts of the central nervous system.
los.html:
• Basal ganglia: deep grey matter nuclei that select and scale movement (start wanted movements, suppress unwanted ones), plus roles in learning habits, motivation and cognition.
ComponentPosition
Caudate nucleusC-shaped, lines the lateral ventricle (head bulges into its anterior horn)
PutamenLateral, outer part of the lentiform nucleus
Globus pallidus (internal and external)Medial part of the lentiform nucleus
Subthalamic nucleusBelow the thalamus
Substantia nigra (pars compacta: dopamine; pars reticulata)Midbrain
  • Striatum = caudate + putamen (input nucleus). Internal capsule separates the caudate and thalamus from the lentiform nucleus.
PathwayRouteEffect
DirectCortex → striatum → GPi (inhibited) → thalamus released → cortexFacilitates movement (dopamine via D1 excites)
IndirectCortex → striatum → GPe → subthalamic nucleus → GPi (excited) → thalamus inhibitedSuppresses movement (dopamine via D2 inhibits)
  • Connections: input from the cortex and substantia nigra (nigrostriatal dopamine)
    • output from GPi/SNr to the thalamus (VA/VL) → motor cortex.
    • No direct spinal output.
DisorderLesionFeatures
Parkinson's diseaseLoss of substantia nigra dopamine neuronsBradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor
Huntington's diseaseCaudate (striatum) atrophyChorea, dementia, psychiatric change
HemiballismusSubthalamic nucleus (lacunar stroke)Wild flinging of the opposite limbs
Wilson's diseaseLentiform nucleus (copper)Tremor, dystonia

los.text: Identify the thalamus and its main functions and connections to other parts of the central nervous system.
los.html:
• Thalamus: paired egg-shaped mass of grey matter in the diencephalon, forming the lateral walls of the 3rd ventricle
    • the main relay to the cortex ("gateway").
NucleusInputOutputFunction
VPL (ventral posterolateral)Dorsal columns (medial lemniscus), spinothalamic tractSomatosensory cortexBody sensation
VPM (ventral posteromedial)Trigeminal pathways, tasteSomatosensory cortexFace sensation, taste
LGN (lateral geniculate)Optic tractVisual cortexVision
MGN (medial geniculate)Inferior colliculusAuditory cortexHearing ("M for music")
VA / VLBasal ganglia, cerebellumMotor and premotor cortexMotor control
AnteriorMammillary bodies (Papez circuit)Cingulate gyrusMemory, emotion
MediodorsalLimbic, amygdalaPrefrontal cortexMood, executive function
Intralaminar, reticularReticular formationDiffuse cortexArousal, attention
  • Smell is the only sense that doesn't relay through the thalamus first.
  • Clinical: thalamic (lacunar) stroke → contralateral sensory loss
    • thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy): severe burning pain on the opposite side
    • bilateral thalamic damage → coma.

los.text: Identify the components of the limbic system, their main functions, and connections to other parts of the central nervous system.
los.html:
• Limbic system: a ring of structures around the corpus callosum and diencephalon controlling emotion, memory, motivation and autonomic/endocrine responses.
ComponentFunction
Hippocampus (medial temporal lobe)Forms new long-term declarative memory
Amygdala (front of the temporal horn)Fear, emotional memory, threat responses
Cingulate gyrusEmotion, pain affect, attention
Parahippocampal gyrus, entorhinal cortexGateway into the hippocampus
FornixMain output of the hippocampus → mammillary bodies
Mammillary bodies (hypothalamus)Memory relay
HypothalamusAutonomic and endocrine output of emotion
Anterior thalamic nucleus, septal nuclei, nucleus accumbensRelay; reward
Papez circuitHippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus → parahippocampal (entorhinal) gyrus → hippocampus.
Connectionsto the prefrontal cortex (decisions), hypothalamus and brainstem (heart rate, sweating, hormones: fight or flight), olfactory system (smell and memory).
DisorderLesionFeatures
Alzheimer's diseaseEarly hippocampus and entorhinal cortex atrophyEarly loss of new memory
Wernicke–Korsakoff (thiamine)Mammillary bodies, medial thalamusAmnesia, confabulation
Herpes simplex encephalitisMedial temporal lobesMemory loss, behaviour change
Kluver–Bucy syndromeBilateral amygdalaHyperorality, hypersexuality, no fear
Temporal lobe epilepsyHippocampal sclerosisDéjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, fear
